messages.author: bbb9357156c132fe
messages.subject: Re: A-matrix feature
parts:
When using the A matrix, the most common mistakes I've made are indexing errors.  If the results look like they've been shuffled around a bit, you should check those!

The problem with the intercept is a bit tricky to explain, but I'll do my best.  What I'm going to describe is a simple version of what the inla.stack() function does, and I suggest that you always use that (instead of programming it yourself), as it's less error prone!

Assume you have a model like  y ~ 1 + height + f(space, model="rw2"), where the covariate height is measured at the data locations (which are NOT on the lattice) and the rw2 effect (space) is specified on a lattice.  You then use an A matrix to link the value of the effect 'space' on the lattice to the interpolated value at the data location.  Because you only want the A matrix to apply  to 'space', you need to be a bit careful.

(NB:: This is an explanation of what would be done naively and does NOT deal with the intercept properly.  See note at end!)

Step 1:  Pad everything with NAs.  Because we have to sections of the problem (the bit on the lattice and the bit off the lattice), we need to separate them somehow.  In R-INLA, we do this by adding NAs to the covariates (and effect indicies) to indicate which bits we want to be ignored.  Keeping with the order of the formula, we will put the off lattice effects (i.e. the covariates) first, and the lattice effects ('space') second.  Set height2 = c(height, rep(NA,length(space)) and space2 = c(rep(NA, length(space)), space).  This makes sure both vectors are of the same length, but have no 'overlapping' components.  The new formula is then y ~ 1 + height2 + f(space2, model = "rw2).

Step 2: Combine the A matrices.   We have two effects of two different sizes (one the length of the data and one the number of nodes in the spatial effect).  To combine them, we need to put two A matrices together.  The first one is an identity matrix (henceforth called Id)  with the same number of rows as the number of data points, and the second one is the matrix linking the spatial effect to the data (which we will call 'Aspace').  Then the combined A matrix stacks these columnwise against each other and the command is control.predictor = list(A = cBind(Id, Aspace) ).  (NB: The capital B in cBind makes sure the result is still a sparse matrix!!)

THE PROBLEM:  The problem is that the default intercept behaviour is (necessarily) stupid and CAN  NOT know that the latent effect has been split with NAs and therefore is of the form c(rep(1, length(height)), rep(1, length(space))).  That is, BOTH A MATRICES WILL PICK UP THE INTERCEPT AND IT WILL APPEAR TWICE! (It's actually worse than this, if the rows of Aspace dont' sum to one, it's impossible to interpret what the actual model is fitting!)

THE SOLUTION: The problem would not exist if instead of a massive vector of ones, the default intercept translated to c( rep(1, length(height)), rep(NA, length(space)) ).  As R cannot know this (an let us all pause to reflect on the stupidity of an automatic default intercept!), we need to do it  ourself.  So we set intercept=o c( rep(1, length(height)), rep(NA, length(space)) ) and make the formula 
     y~ intercept + height + f(space, model="rw2)-1

I hope this explanation helped.  As you can see, this will not occur every single time you use the A matrix and a formula, but when it does, it can be devastating.  The best solution is to never rely on the default intercept, but the best that we can do is put a strong warning in the code that something may have gone terribly terribly wrong.

messages.author: bbb9357156c132fe
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: A-matrix feature
parts:
Ah!  Ok.   That's my fault - I chose the parameter values poorly.  

The problem is that the estimated spatial scale of the problem (and the TRUE scale of the simulated problem) is larger than the domain.  In this case, the field is essentially intrinsic and it's difficult to separate the non-zero mean of the posterior spatial effect from the intercept.  If you run the model with a larger value of kappa, it will work fine!

In this case, using the default intercept is not a mistake as there are no covariates/effects at different spatial locations.

/D
